name: dbt
license: Apache 2.0 (dbt v1, and the source of dbt v2 built as `dbt-oss`); the default dbt v2 binary adds proprietary features under the dbt product licence; the dbt platform is proprietary SaaS
summary: SQL `select` statements in git, built into warehouse tables in dependency order, with tests and docs alongside.
intro: A dbt project is a folder of models, each a `.sql` file holding one `select`, plus YAML files with tests and descriptions. dbt runs wherever you start it: a laptop, a CI job or a scheduler. It renders the Jinja in each model, swaps `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}` for the real table name, and builds a dependency graph from those references. It then sends `create table as`, `create view` or `merge` statements to the warehouse through an adapter, in graph order, so the warehouse does all the work and the data never passes through dbt. Data tests are queries that return failing rows; `dbt build` runs models and tests together and skips everything downstream of a failed test. `dbt docs generate` writes a static site with the lineage graph.

There are two engines. dbt v1 is the original Python program (`dbt-core` plus one adapter package per warehouse), Apache 2.0 and still maintained. dbt v2, released on 14 September 2026, is a Rust rewrite that grew out of the Fusion engine and ships as one binary. Its source is Apache 2.0 and installs as `dbt-oss`; the default `dbt` distribution adds proprietary SQL comprehension (errors caught before the warehouse runs anything, editor autocomplete, `dbt lint`) and is free to use. The hosted dbt platform, formerly dbt Cloud, adds scheduling, CI, a browser IDE and a catalog: Developer is free for one seat and 3,000 successful model builds a month, Starter is $100 per seat per month with five developer seats and 15,000 builds, and Enterprise is priced by quote (checked 6 October 2026). dbt Labs merged with Fivetran in June 2026; dbt continues as its own brand.
strengths: Plain SQL plus Jinja: anyone who writes `select` statements can build models, and `ref()` works out the build order
Software habits for analytics: models live in git, run in CI and carry tests and descriptions next to the code
Runs on the warehouse you already have, through adapters for Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, DuckDB and, on v1, Postgres and many community adapters
Widely supported: Dagster, Fabric Data Factory and Fivetran all run dbt projects
Open-source core under Apache 2.0, and v2 installs as a single binary with no Python environment to manage
limits: Only the T: dbt doesn’t extract or load data, so you still need a loader (Fivetran, Airbyte, CDC) and usually an orchestrator

A version in transition: v2 is stricter at parse time and supports fewer warehouses so far (BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, Snowflake and DuckDB GA; Spark beta; ClickHouse private beta); Postgres stays on v1
Layered licensing: the source is Apache 2.0, but the default v2 binary includes proprietary code, and products that embed it must let users sign in to the dbt platform
Every run is warehouse compute: full rebuilds of big models add up, which is why incremental models exist and why dbt sells dbt State ($0.094 per daily active target table) to skip unchanged ones

sections.title: Other ways to do the T

items.name: SQLMesh
items.text: A transformation framework that is compatible with dbt projects, with a plan and apply workflow and virtual development environments. Built by Tobiko Data, which Fivetran bought in 2025; now a Linux Foundation project.

items.name: Dataform
items.text: SQLX files with `ref()` and assertions, compiled and run inside BigQuery. A managed service tied to BigQuery.

items.name: Bruin
items.text: One Go binary for ingestion, SQL and Python transforms and quality checks, so a small team can skip a separate loader.

items.name: dbt jobs in Fabric
items.text: Fabric Data Factory can build, test and deploy dbt models on a Fabric data warehouse without running dbt yourself.

story: In 2015 and 2016 a team at RJMetrics wrote down a viewpoint: analytics teams had “a workflow problem”, and the practices software engineers use, such as version control, testing and separate environments, should apply to analytics code. Cloud warehouses such as Redshift could now hold raw data and do the heavy lifting, but the SQL that turned it into reports lived in scattered scripts and BI tools.

Tristan Handy started Fishtown Analytics in Philadelphia in 2016 as a consulting business. dbt’s first commit landed that March, and Handy and co-founder Drew Banin released it as a productivity tool for the consulting work. It was narrow on purpose: “dbt is the T in ELT”, Handy wrote in 2017. It doesn’t move data; it turns `select` statements into tables inside the warehouse, in the right order. A community grew around its Slack channel, and in June 2021 the company renamed itself dbt Labs while raising $150 million. dbt 1.0 followed that December.

In January 2025 dbt Labs bought SDF Labs, whose Rust SQL compiler became the Fusion engine, announced that May under the source-available Elastic License. After the merger with Fivetran closed on 1 June 2026, the Rust engine became dbt v2.0 under Apache 2.0 in September 2026.

choices.why: Analysts already knew SQL. dbt generates the `create`, `insert` and `merge` statements for each warehouse from the model’s materialization, so the model holds only the logic.
References give dbt the dependency graph, so it can build in order and draw lineage. The same code also points at a developer’s schema or production depending on the environment.
Cloud warehouses were powerful enough to do the work, so dbt stayed out of extraction and loading and let the warehouse compute everything.

choices.choice: Open source, controlled by its users
choices.why: Handy wrote that “critical analytics infrastructure should be controlled by its users as open source software”. The core has stayed Apache 2.0; the 2025 Fusion engine’s Elastic License was dropped when its code became dbt v2.
